claims.text: A defect-aware model incorporating oxygen interstitials and alloy disorder will predict bulk HfNbTaTiZr conductivity more accurately than perfect-crystal analytical approaches across 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
The relevant bulk HfNbTaTiZr specimen contains approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
Approximately 1 wt.% oxygen in HfNbTaTiZr produces interstitial oxygen defects.
Interstitial oxygen modifies the local electronic structure and acts as a charge-carrier scattering center, thereby reducing or otherwise altering mobility.
Alloy disorder contributes to electrical scattering in HfNbTaTiZr.
Quantum transport phenomena, including weak localization and defect-induced scattering, dominate conductivity in the 0–200 K regime.
Additional scattering from oxygen can induce or alter weak localization at low temperature.
Phonon scattering and oxygen-mediated effects are significant from 300 to 1200 K.
At high temperature, oxygen defects enhance electron-phonon scattering and may locally modify oxidation states.
The coherent potential approximation provides a quantum-mechanical treatment of solid-solution disorder.
Machine-learning interatomic-potential methods can treat defects and local atomic relaxations better than CPA.
Combining CPA-like quantum calculations with machine-learning corrections should improve accuracy by jointly treating alloy disorder and oxygen defects.
The defect-aware model will reduce conductivity-prediction error by more than 20% relative to conventional defect-free models in both temperature regimes.
Existing perfect-crystal analytical models show notable deviations from measured conductivity in oxygen-contaminated HfNbTaTiZr.

The model is applicable to bulk HfNbTaTiZr near 1 wt.% oxygen over 0–200 K and 300–1200 K, but may not be valid for substantially purer or more contaminated specimens or outside those temperature ranges.
Annealing HfNbTaTiZr in a reducing atmosphere can provide a near-defect-free comparison specimen.
Oxygen-containing and near-defect-free HfNbTaTiZr specimens should exhibit systematic differences in electrical conductivity.
Failure to improve prediction error by at least 20% in both temperature regimes, or failure to observe the predicted systematic specimen differences, is designated as falsifying the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The stated applicability boundary says predictions may not be valid for ultra-high-purity specimens, yet the proposed falsification experiment evaluates the model against a near-defect-free specimen without defining a separate valid model or benchmark for that condition.
